articles.title: Record What Your Code Throws Before You Refactor It
articles.excerpt: Most refactors keep the happy path intact. They quietly rewrite the error path. Messages get reworded. Exception types get normalized. Validation order flips. Reviewers read the new structure, not the…
articles.body: Most refactors keep the happy path intact. They quietly rewrite the error path. Messages get reworded. Exception types get normalized. Validation order flips. Reviewers read the new structure, not the old failure output. Freeze those three things before you extract anything. Why the error path drifts A helper extraction moves two raise statements into one place. The first error now wins. Nothing fails, tests stay green, and your logs change shape. Happy-path tests never reach those branches. So they cannot notice. The fix is not more assertions. It is a recorded baseline of observable failures, replayed after each small change. Step 1: Put the imperfect module on the table Here is a realistic messy function. Validation, pricing, and coupon lookup are welded together.
articles.author: Dakota Huang

articles.title: Which Gate Should Run First? Ordering Agent-Patch Checks by Yield per Second
articles.excerpt: Gate order is a cost decision, not a taste decision. If your most expensive check runs first, you pay full-suite prices for diffs that a scope read would have routed differently in under a second. Thi…
articles.body: Gate order is a cost decision, not a taste decision. If your most expensive check runs first, you pay full-suite prices for diffs that a scope read would have routed differently in under a second. This post treats the ordering itself as the artifact: a three-tier ladder, a verdict model that distinguishes failure from inconclusive, and an evidence rule for freezing flaky tests instead of freezing them by reflex. It does not re-argue whether fixture edits need their own gate — I have written about that separately. Here the question is narrower: given several checks you already trust, which one do you run, in what order, and how do you know the order is working? The ordering mistake that hides in plain sight A test suite is not a single check.
articles.author: Finley Zhou

articles.title: Your Docs Gate Has Never Failed, So It Proves Nothing: Mutation-Testing a Model-Drafted Page
articles.excerpt: A documentation gate that has only ever printed pass is not evidence of quality; it is evidence that nobody has tried to break it. Before you let a free model draft a page into a review queue, spend t…
articles.body: A documentation gate that has only ever printed pass is not evidence of quality; it is evidence that nobody has tried to break it. Before you let a free model draft a page into a review queue, spend twenty minutes proving that your checks actually reject bad drafts. This post builds a small gate, then a mutation harness that injects known defects and asserts the gate fails on each one. The conclusion up front: the mutation sheet, not the gate, is the artifact that tells you which parts of the page a human still has to own. 1. The failure mode this fixes Most AI-drafting pipelines fail in the same quiet way: the checker looks for things the model already produces.

articles.title: Probabilistic Graph Neural Inference for sustainable aquaculture monitoring systems during mission-critical recovery windows
articles.excerpt: Probabilistic Graph Neural Inference for sustainable aquaculture monitoring systems during mission-critical recovery windows Introduction: A Sensor Failure That Changed My Research Direction Last spri…
articles.body: Probabilistic Graph Neural Inference for sustainable aquaculture monitoring systems during mission-critical recovery windows Introduction: A Sensor Failure That Changed My Research Direction Last spring, I was running a small experimental setup to study how machine learning models behave under sensor degradation. I had deployed a handful of cheap IoT water-quality sensors across a friend's tilapia pond — dissolved oxygen probes, temperature loggers, turbidity meters — and piped everything into a time-series anomaly detector I'd been tinkering with for months. The model worked beautifully for six weeks. Then a storm knocked out three sensors simultaneously, and my entire inference pipeline collapsed into a cascade of garbage predictions.

articles.title: White-labelled AI tools: is your agency the provider under the AI Act?
articles.excerpt: This guide was drafted by an AI agent from the primary sources linked at the bottom, and has not been reviewed by a lawyer. It is general information, not legal advice. The original is at https://mdod…
articles.body: This guide was drafted by an AI agent from the primary sources linked at the bottom, and has not been reviewed by a lawyer. It is general information, not legal advice. The original is at https://mdodeja.github.io/eu-ai-act-article-50-guide/guides/white-label-ai-tools-provider-article-50.html . Short answer. Possibly. The AI Act's provider is whoever develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. An agency that sells a vendor's chatbot as "AgencyBot" fits that wording more closely than one that installs the vendor's branded widget for a client. If you are the provider, the Article 50(1) duty to design the chatbot so people know it is an AI is yours, even though the vendor wrote the code.

articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.excerpt: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.body: I have been dreaming of doing research in space as an astronaut my whole life, but for some reason, the thought of working underwater made me nervous. I’ve known for a long time that astronauts train underwater to simulate different scenarios they’re likely to experience in space. Diving was never an issue for me, either — I even made it as far as becoming a certified rescue diver. So what was the problem? This summer, I led a simulated space mission in an underwater habitat called the Jules’ Undersea Lab. It is a research station that is located 22 feet (6.7 meters) underwater near Key Largo, Florida. You have to scuba dive to get in and out of the station. To become an aquanaut , you have to stay underwater for at least 24 hours in a so-called state of saturation.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 26, 2004: Cassini spacecraft takes 1st-ever closeup photos of Saturn moon Titan
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. The Cassini spacecraft would later drop off a probe on Titan named Huygens, which was a European spacecraft that hitched a ride to the Saturn system with the Cassini mission. But before Cassini dropped off its robotic passenger, it flew by Titan a few times and took some amazing photos . Cassini completed its first flyby on July 3, 2004, but when it swung by a second time on Oct. 26, it got about 300 times closer than it did the first time. At the closest point of this flyby, Cassini was 745 miles (1,200 kilometers) away from the surface of Titan. The spacecraft took hundreds of photos during this flyby , and these were the highest resolution views of Titan anyone had ever seen.
